unit.comment: The unit type and its sole value are both written `$` (analogous to () in Rust/ML). Highlighted like the other built-in types.
unit.name: support.type.builtin.unit.quilon

type-names.comment: Capitalized identifiers are types / sum-type constructors (Ok, NotOk, Color, Circle).
type-names.name: entity.name.type.quilon

function-calls.comment: lowercase identifier immediately followed by ( is a function call

collection-fences.comment: The `[| … |]` fence around a map/set literal (`[|"a" => 1|]`, `[|1, 2|]`). `[` on its own is unscoped and `|` is the match operator (scoped in #operators), so without this rule the two halves of the fence would color differently; scoping `[|`/`|]` as one punctuation token each, in the same family as the block-delimiter scopes, keeps the fence visually one thing. Listed before #operators so `|` inside the fence tokenizes as part of it rather than as the match operator, and `||` (logical-and's sibling) is unaffected — this only matches the two-character `[|`/`|]` pairs.

operators.comment: TextMate applies, at each position, the FIRST pattern in this list that matches there — ties at the same start position are NOT broken by length. So every multi-character operator MUST be listed before the single-character rules, and before any single-char operator that is a prefix of it (e.g. `||` before `|`, `<=` before `<`, `=>`/`==` before `=`). That ordering is what keeps a two-char operator from being split into its first character + the rest. Each multi-char operator is its own scope.

patterns.comment: == != <= >= — listed before `=`, `!`, `<`, `>` so a two-char comparison is never split into its first char + the rest.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.comparison.quilon

patterns.comment: && || — the two-char logical operators, listed before the single-char `!` and `|` below.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.logical.quilon

patterns.comment: Block delimiters, scoped so the opening `<` and closing `>` of a `< … >` block share the `punctuation.definition.block` family and a theme colors them the same — not as an error/operator. The closing `>` half follows the compiler's rule (see docs/expressions/README.md): a `>` closes a block unless an operand follows it on the same line, so the negative lookahead lists the characters an operand can start with. The opening `<` half is a highlighting heuristic — the compiler always lexes `<` as block-open and recovers less-than in the parser, which a stateless grammar can't do; so we approximate block-open as a line-final `<`, which is how a canonical multi-line block opens. These are listed BEFORE `[<>]` so a delimiter wins. `<=`/`>=`/`<-`/`->`/`<<`/`>>` are unaffected — those multi-char rules match earlier. Fully correct block `< >` vs comparison `<`/`>` coloring is impossible in a context-free TextMate grammar and is deferred to semantic tokens / an LSP; these lookaheads are the safe best-effort.
patterns.name: punctuation.definition.block.begin.quilon
